goldens.comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

golden_verdicts.matched_finding: updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data {} relies on implicit Prisma @updatedAt behavior
golden_verdicts.reason: F14 and F19 both identify the same issue: updateManyByCredentialId is called with empty data object {}, relying on Prisma's @updatedAt implicit behavior, and suggest explicitly setting updatedAt: new Date()

golden_verdicts.matched_finding: sed -i '' is BSD-only; breaks on GNU sed (Linux)
golden_verdicts.reason: F6 identifies the exact same issue: sed -i '' syntax is BSD/macOS-specific and fails on GNU sed/Linux systems, at the same location in scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh

findings.blocking_reason: This is a new feature that partially no-ops due to cache regeneration from an active webhook, but it is not a security vulnerability, data loss, regression, or contract break — it is a logic/UX design issue with a newly added handler.
findings.body:
**The new `deleteCache` handler performs only step 1 of the 3-step canonical lifecycle that `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar` established.** This is a silent logic error: the user clicks "Delete cached data", sees a success toast ("Cache deleted successfully"), but within seconds of the next Google Calendar event change the cache is silently recreated by the webhook handler. The feature is effectively a no-op for every Google Calendar user with an active webhook subscription — which is the default state after installing the Google Calendar app.

**The canonical 3-step lifecycle** (in `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar`, lines 954–967):
1. `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` — delete cache rows
2. `this.stopWatchingCalendarsInGoogle(allChannelsForThisCalendarBeingUnwatched)` — call Google Calendar API `channels.stop` with `{ id, resourceId }` tuples stored on `SelectedCalendar` rows, so Google stops sending push notifications
3. `this.upsertSelectedCalendarsForEventTypeIds({ ..., googleChannelId: null, googleChannelResourceId: null, googleChannelResourceUri: null, googleChannelExpiration: null, googleChannelKind: null }, ...)` — null out the channel metadata on `SelectedCalendar` rows so the webhook handler can no longer look them up

**The new `deleteCache` handler** (lines 28–30) performs **only step 1**. It does not call `stopWatchingCalendarsInGoogle`, and it does not null out `SelectedCalendar.googleChannelId`. Both the Google channel and the `SelectedCalendar` channel metadata remain intact.

**The regeneration path is confirmed end-to-end**:
- `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/api/webhook.ts` line 31: `SelectedCalendarRepository.findFirstByGoogleChannelId(channelId)` looks up the `SelectedCalendar` by the `googleChannelId` that Google sends in the `x-goog-channel-id` header. Since `deleteCache` did not null out `googleChannelId`, this lookup still succeeds.
- webhook.ts line 46: `await calendarServiceForCalendarCache?.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache?.(selectedCalendars)` — fetches fresh availability from Google and calls `setAvailabilityInCache`, which calls `calendarCache.upsertCachedAvailability({ credentialId, userId, args, value })` (CalendarService.ts line 979–988). This **re-creates the `CalendarCache` row** that `deleteCache` just deleted.

**Observable user-facing behavior**: User clicks "Delete cached data" → success toast → cache momentarily empty → next Google push (within seconds to minutes of any calendar event change) → cache repopulated with identical data. The UI in `CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx` does not communicate this — the confirmation dialog (`t("confirm_delete_cache")`) and success toast (`t("cache_deleted_successfully")`) both imply permanent deletion.

**Orphaned channel blast radius**: Because `stopWatchingCalendarsInGoogle` is never called, the Google webhook channel remains active indefinitely. Google will continue sending push notifications to `/api/integrations/googlecalendar/webhook` for every event change on that calendar, consuming Google API quota and triggering cache regeneration on every push. The only way for the user to stop this is to go through the full disconnect flow (which correctly calls `unwatchCalendar`). There is no UI path to stop the channel without disconnecting the entire integration.

**The `SelectedCalendar.googleChannelId` remains non-null**: This orphans the channel metadata — the webhook handler can still find the `SelectedCalendar` and regenerate cache, but the user has no way to stop the channel short of disconnecting the integration. The `googleChannelId` / `googleChannelResourceId` tuple needed to call `channels.stop` is preserved on `SelectedCalendar` rows but nothing in the `deleteCache` flow uses it.
findings.evidence:
Step 1 (deleteCache.handler.ts:28-30): `await prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` — only step 1 of the canonical lifecycle.
Step 2 (CalendarService.ts:954-967): The canonical `unwatchCalendar` performs 3 ordered steps: (1) `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })`, (2) `this.stopWatchingCalendarsInGoogle(allChannelsForThisCalendarBeingUnwatched)`, (3) `this.upsertSelectedCalendarsForEventTypeIds({ ..., googleChannelId: null, googleChannelResourceId: null, ... }, eventTypeIdsToBeUnwatched)`. `deleteCache` does only step 1.
Step 3 (CalendarService.ts:126-146): `stopWatchingCalendarsInGoogle` calls `calendar.channels.stop({ requestBody: { resourceId: googleChannelResourceId, id: googleChannelId } })` for each unique channel — this is the Google API call that stops push notifications. `deleteCache` never calls this, so the channel stays active.
Step 4 (webhook.ts:31): `const selectedCalendar = await SelectedCalendarRepository.findFirstByGoogleChannelId(channelId)` — after `deleteCache`, `SelectedCalendar.googleChannelId` is still non-null, so this lookup succeeds when Google sends the next push.
Step 5 (webhook.ts:46): `await calendarServiceForCalendarCache?.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache?.(selectedCalendars)` — calls `setAvailabilityInCache` (CalendarService.ts:979-988) which calls `calendarCache.upsertCachedAvailability({ credentialId, userId, args, value })`, re-creating the `CalendarCache` row that `deleteCache` deleted.
Step 6 (CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx:42-50): `deleteCacheMutation` shows `t("cache_deleted_successfully")` toast on success — implies permanent deletion. No `onSettled` to invalidate `connectedCalendars`, so the cache-status timestamp in the dropdown won't even refresh without a manual page reload.
Result: The "Delete cached data" button is a silent no-op for any user with an active Google webhook subscription. The cache regenerates on the next Google push, and the Google channel is orphaned (consuming API quota with no way to stop it short of full disconnect).
findings.suggestion:
Two valid approaches, depending on intended semantics:

**Option A (recommended — match `unwatchCalendar` semantics):** If "Delete cached data" is meant to actually clear the cache and keep it cleared, the handler should perform the full 3-step lifecycle that `unwatchCalendar` does, or better, delegate to `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar` itself (or a shared helper extracted from it). Specifically:
1. `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` (already present)
2. Look up `SelectedCalendar` rows for this `credentialId` that have non-null `googleChannelId` / `googleChannelResourceId`, and call `CalendarService.stopWatchingCalendarsInGoogle(channels)` with those tuples.
3. Null out `SelectedCalendar.googleChannelId` / `googleChannelResourceId` / `googleChannelResourceUri` / `googleChannelExpiration` / `googleChannelKind` via `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId` (the method this PR already added) or `upsertSelectedCalendarsForEventTypeIds`.

**Option B (if cache regeneration is intended):** If the intent is genuinely "clear the cache now, let it regenerate on next push", then the UI must communicate this. The confirmation dialog and success toast should say something like "Cache will be refreshed when Google Calendar sends the next update" rather than "Cache deleted successfully", and the `cache_deleted_successfully` locale string should be updated accordingly. This option still leaves the orphaned-channel quota concern unaddressed, so Option A is strongly preferred.

In both cases, the handler should also invalidate the `connectedCalendars` TRPC query (the `deleteCacheMutation` in `CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx` has no `onSettled` / `utils.invalidate()` call, unlike the adjacent `disconnectMutation`), so the UI cache-status timestamp actually refreshes after deletion.
findings.title: deleteCache breaks the cache-channel lifecycle pairing — cache silently regenerates from the still-active Google webhook

findings.blocking_reason: This is a functionality completeness gap, not a security vulnerability, data loss, API contract break, or demonstrated regression of previously working behavior.
findings.body: The deleteCache handler only calls `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` to remove cached calendar data, but does NOT stop the associated Google Calendar webhook channel. The existing `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar` method correctly pairs cache deletion with channel stop (`stopChannel` + `deleteCache`). By bypassing this, the webhook remains active and the next push from Google will silently recreate the cache rows, making the 'clear cache' operation a no-op for any user with an active webhook subscription.
findings.evidence: deleteCache.handler.ts line 27: `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })`. No call to `unwatchCalendar`, `stopChannel`, or any Google webhook API. Compare with CalendarService.unwatchCalendar which does both `stopChannel` and `deleteCache` atomically.
findings.suggestion: In deleteCache.handler.ts, before or after deleting the cache, call the appropriate webhook stop method. Ideally use `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar` or at minimum stop the Google channel via the googleChannelId. Alternatively, if stopping the webhook is out of scope for this PR, document the limitation and consider whether the cache should be cleared at all when a webhook is active.
findings.title: deleteCache handler doesn't stop Google webhook channel - cache silently regenerates

findings.blocking_reason: This is a UX staleness issue (stale timestamp shown after successful server-side deletion) — not a build break, security vulnerability, data loss, API contract break, or regression of previously working behavior.
findings.body:
The `deleteCacheMutation` (lines 42-50) only defines `onSuccess` (shows a toast and calls `onSuccess?.()`) and `onError`. It does **not** invalidate the tRPC query that supplies the `cacheUpdatedAt` prop rendered in this very component.

Contrast this with the sibling `disconnectMutation` (lines 53-65) in the same file, which correctly defines `onSettled` to invalidate both `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `utils.viewer.apps.integrations`.

**Why this matters:** The `cacheUpdatedAt` timestamp displayed in the dropdown (lines 86-95) is sourced from the `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query — the PR's `connectedCalendarsHandler` enriches calendar data with cache status via `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`. When the user clicks "Delete cached data" and the mutation succeeds, the server-side cache row is deleted, but the React Query cache for `connectedCalendars` is **not** invalidated. The component continues to render the now-stale `cacheUpdatedAt` timestamp (and the `hasCache` branch keeps the "Cache Status" / "Delete cached data" UI visible) until the query is refetched by some unrelated trigger (page reload, window refocus, or another mutation that happens to invalidate it).

This produces a confusing UX where the user is told "Cache deleted successfully" via toast, yet the dropdown still shows the old "Cache last updated" timestamp and continues to offer the "Delete cached data" action as if nothing happened. The user cannot visually confirm the deletion occurred, and may re-trigger the delete unnecessarily.

**Reachability:** The component is rendered for every Google Calendar credential with `cacheUpdatedAt` set (line 69: `hasCache = isGoogleCalendar && cacheUpdatedAt`). The delete flow is triggered by the confirmation dialog at lines 130-141 calling `deleteCacheMutation.mutate({ credentialId })`. This is a primary, user-facing action — not an edge case.
findings.evidence:
Step 1: User opens the dropdown for a Google Calendar credential with `cacheUpdatedAt` set (line 69 `hasCache = isGoogleCalendar && cacheUpdatedAt` evaluates truthy).
Step 2: User clicks "Delete cached data" → confirmation dialog `onConfirm` fires `deleteCacheMutation.mutate({ credentialId })` (line 136).
Step 3: Mutation succeeds server-side → `onSuccess` (lines 43-46) runs: shows toast `cache_deleted_successfully` and calls `onSuccess?.()`. No query invalidation occurs. `onError` (lines 47-49) only shows a toast. There is no `onSettled` callback on `deleteCacheMutation`.
Step 4: The `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` React Query cache is unchanged — it still holds the pre-delete response where `cacheUpdatedAt` was a valid Date.
Step 5: The component re-renders with the same `cacheUpdatedAt` prop → `hasCache` (line 69) remains truthy → the "Cache Status" row (lines 84-97) continues rendering the stale timestamp, and the "Delete cached data" menu item (lines 98-109) remains visible.
Step 6: Compare with `disconnectMutation` (lines 53-65): its `onSettled` (lines 61-64) calls `await utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` and `await utils.viewer.apps.integrations.invalidate()`, which is the correct pattern. `deleteCacheMutation` is missing this exact invalidation.
findings.title: deleteCacheMutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars — stale cacheUpdatedAt persists in UI after cache delete

findings.blocking_reason: I18n locale consistency issue is a code quality/UX concern, not a build break, security vulnerability, data loss, API contract break, or regression of existing behavior.
findings.body:
The new i18n key `cache_last_updated` (added in `common.json` line 3382) uses `{{timestamp}}` interpolation, but the value passed to it is formatted with a hardcoded `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` at line 89 of `CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx`. This means the `cache_last_updated` string will display in the user's language (once translated) but the timestamp itself will always be in US English format (e.g., "6/30/2026, 3:45 PM").

The codebase convention is to use `i18n.language` from the `useLocale()` hook. Six other components follow this pattern:
- `TroubleshooterHeader.tsx`: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language, ...)`
- `DateOverrideList.tsx`: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language, ...)`
- `DateValues/index.tsx`: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language, ...)`
- `Header.tsx`: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language ?? "en", ...)`
- `DatePicker.tsx`: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language, ...)`
- `dates.tsx`: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(language, ...)`

The `useLocale()` hook (in `packages/lib/hooks/useLocale.ts`) already returns `i18n` which has the `.language` property, but `CredentialActionsDropdown` only destructures `t` — it does not access `i18n.language`.

This affects all non-en-US users: a German user would see "Zuletzt aktualisiert: 6/30/2026, 3:45 PM" (mixed language) instead of "Zuletzt aktualisiert: 30.6.2026, 15:45".
findings.evidence:
Step 1: `CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx` line 37: `const { t } = useLocale();` — only destructures `t`, not `i18n`.
Step 2: Line 89: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" }).format(new Date(cacheUpdatedAt))` — hardcodes `"en-US"` instead of using `i18n.language`.
Step 3: The formatted string is passed as `timestamp` to `t("cache_last_updated", { timestamp: ... })` at line 88.
Step 4: The i18n key `cache_last_updated` (common.json line 3382) embeds this value: `"Last updated: {{timestamp}}"`.
Step 5: For a German user with `i18n.language = "de"`, the label translates to German but the timestamp remains in en-US format, producing mixed-language output.
Step 6: Contrast with `DateOverrideList.tsx` line 52: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language, ...)` — the established convention.
findings.title: Hardcoded `en-US` locale in `Intl.DateTimeFormat` breaks i18n for `cache_last_updated` key

findings.blocking_reason: Architectural concern about incomplete teardown does not demonstrate a regression, data loss, or broken contract; the cache being repopulated is a functional design issue, not production-irreversible damage.
findings.body: Uses raw `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany` instead of `CalendarCacheRepository`. The repository's `unwatchCalendar` flow (CalendarService.ts line 895) does 6 steps: find selectedCalendars → check other watchers → delete cache → stop Google webhook channel → null channel fields. `deleteCache.handler` replicates only step 3 (cache delete), leaving the Google webhook active — it will re-push and repopulate the cache, making "Delete cache" a transient reset rather than the teardown the UI label implies.
findings.title: Repository pattern bypass + incomplete teardown

findings.blocking_reason: Incomplete cache-clearing behavior is a functional bug, not a regression or data-loss/security issue — the finding doesn't establish this PR removed previously-working channel-stop logic.
findings.body:
By omitting the channel-stop half, `deleteCache` leaves the Google push channel active AND leaves `googleChannelId` on `SelectedCalendar` intact. The webhook handler (`webhook.ts` L31) then still resolves the calendar by channel ID and L46 regenerates the exact cache rows just deleted — making "Clear cache" a no-op for any Google credential with an active webhook (the common case). Secondary issue: leaked channel subscription on Google's side.

All three false-positive gates passed:
- **Reachability**: webhook.ts is the live Google push endpoint; `findFirstByGoogleChannelId` is the documented lookup path.
- **Evidence chain**: 6-step trace from deleteCache → active channel → push → cache regen, each step sourced to specific lines.
- **Confidence**: 0.9 — direct code reading of both the bypass and the canonical pairing.
findings.evidence: 6-step trace from deleteCache → active channel → push → cache regen, each step sourced to specific lines.
findings.title: deleteCache leaves Google push channel active, making Clear cache a no-op

findings.blocking_reason: Shell script portability issue is a developer-experience problem, not a build/test/security/data/API contract regression in production-running code.
findings.body: Line 68 uses `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|...|"` which is BSD sed syntax (the empty string after `-i` means "no backup file"). On GNU sed (Linux), `sed -i ''` interprets `''` as the sed script to execute, producing a syntax error: `sed: -e expression #1, char 0: no previous regular expression`. The same repo's `deploy/install.sh` uses GNU sed syntax (`sed -i 's|...|...|g'` with no `''`), so the new script is inconsistent with existing conventions and will fail for any Linux developer. Since the script is a dev helper that contributors may run on either OS, a portable approach is needed.
findings.suggestion: Use a portable sed invocation. Either: (a) detect the platform and branch: `if [[ "$(uname)" == "Darwin" ]]; then sed -i '' -E "..." "$ENV_FILE"; else sed -i -E "..." "$ENV_FILE"; fi`, or (b) use a temp file + `sed -E "..." "$ENV_FILE" > "$ENV_FILE.tmp" && mv "$ENV_FILE.tmp" "$ENV_FILE"` which works on both, or (c) use perl: `perl -pi -e 's|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|' "$ENV_FILE"`.
findings.title: sed -i '' is BSD-only; breaks on GNU sed (Linux)

findings.blocking_reason: Hardcoded locale in date formatting is a code quality/i18n improvement, not a security, data-loss, build, or API-contract break.
findings.body: The component hardcodes `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { year: "numeric", month: "short", day: "numeric", hour: "2-digit", minute: "2-digit" })` to format the cache timestamp. This ignores the user's selected locale. Cal.com uses next-i18next and provides a `useLocale()` hook. All other date formatting in the codebase uses the user's locale.
findings.evidence: CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`. The i18n keys were correctly added to common.json but the date formatter ignores locale.
findings.suggestion: Import `useLocale` from `@/lib/i18n` (or appropriate next-i18next hook) and use the returned locale: `const locale = useLocale(); new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { ... })`.
findings.title: Hardcoded en-US locale in Intl.DateTimeFormat ignores user locale

findings.blocking_reason: UI staleness after cache deletion is a UX issue, not data loss, security vulnerability, build break, or regression of a previously working behavior.
findings.body: The `deleteCacheMutation` has `onSuccess` and `onError` callbacks but no `onSettled` callback to invalidate the `connectedCalendars` query. After cache deletion, the `cacheUpdatedAt` field in the UI will still show the old timestamp because the query data is stale. The sibling `disconnectMutation` correctly invalidates `connectedCalendars` in its `onSettled`, showing the intended pattern.
findings.evidence: deleteCacheMutation: `onSuccess: () => { showToast(...) }, onError: () => { showToast(...) }` - no onSettled. disconnectMutation: `onSettled: () => { utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate(); utils.viewer.credentials.invalidate() }` - correct pattern.
findings.suggestion: Add `onSettled: () => { utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate(); }` to the deleteCacheMutation. Optionally also invalidate any other queries that depend on cache status.
findings.title: deleteCacheMutation missing onSettled - connectedCalendars query not invalidated

findings.blocking_reason: Architectural critique about repository pattern consistency with no demonstrated production impact.
findings.body: The handler directly calls `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` instead of using the `CalendarCacheRepository`. The repository pattern is established in this codebase - `CalendarCacheRepository` already exists with a `deleteManyByCredential` method. Bypassing it breaks the abstraction and makes future changes (like adding webhook stop logic) harder to centralize.
findings.evidence: deleteCache.handler.ts: `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })`. CalendarCacheRepository has `deleteManyByCredential(credentialId: number)` method. The connectedCalendars.handler.ts correctly uses `new CalendarCacheRepository()` for cache status queries.
findings.suggestion: Replace `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` with `new CalendarCacheRepository().deleteManyByCredential(credentialId)`. Or inject the repository instance.
findings.title: deleteCacheHandler uses raw Prisma bypassing repository pattern

findings.blocking_reason: Throwing a generic Error instead of TRPCError is a code-quality/error-handling improvement; access control still works and it doesn't break the build or regress behavior.
findings.body: When the credential is not found or doesn't belong to the user, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In a tRPC context, this should be `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND", message: "..." })` or `UNAUTHORIZED`. Generic errors are caught by tRPC's error handler and presented as internal server errors with code `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR`, which is misleading.
findings.evidence: deleteCache.handler.ts: `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. Other handlers in the codebase use `TRPCError` from `@trpc/server`.
findings.suggestion: Import `TRPCError` from `@calcom/trpc/server/trpc` or `@trpc/server` and use: `throw new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND", message: "Credential not found or access denied" })`.
findings.title: deleteCacheHandler throws generic Error instead of TRPCError

findings.blocking_reason: Missing tests for new feature code does not break the build, tests, or type-checking and falls under the non-blocking category of missing test coverage.
findings.body: No test files exist for any of the new code: no tests for `deleteCache.handler.ts`, `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` repository method, `CredentialActionsDropdown` component, or the `updateManyByCredentialId` repository method. The mock repository (`calendar-cache.repository.mock.ts`) was added but no tests use it.
findings.evidence: Searched for `deleteCache.test`, `CredentialActionsDropdown.test`, `calendar-cache.repository.test` - no files found. The mock repository file exists but is unused.
findings.suggestion: Add unit tests for the repository method (especially edge cases: empty array, expired cache). Add integration test for deleteCache handler (authorization, success path). Add component test for CredentialActionsDropdown (mutation calls, loading states, query invalidation).
findings.title: No tests for new feature code

findings.blocking_reason: Feature-flag bypass causes UI confusion for a disabled feature but no data loss (deleteCache is a no-op per the finding), no security vulnerability, no broken API contract, and not a demonstrated regression of previously working behavior.
findings.body: connectedCalendars.handler.ts:28 directly constructs `new CalendarCacheRepository()`, bypassing the `CalendarCache.init` factory (calendar-cache.ts:22-29) which checks `isCalendarCacheEnabledGlobally`. When the feature flag is OFF, all other code paths receive `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` — meaning no real cache rows are written. However, the migration `20250715160635_add_calendar_cache_updated_at` (migration.sql:9) backfills `updatedAt = NOW()` for all pre-existing CalendarCache rows. The compound escalation: (1) the feature flag is OFF, so no new cache rows are written via the mock; (2) but pre-migration rows still exist in the real CalendarCache table with backfilled `updatedAt` timestamps; (3) the bypassed handler queries the real table and returns these orphaned rows; (4) getCacheStatusByCredentialIds (calendar-cache.repository.ts:173-188) applies no `expiresAt` filter, so even expired/old rows are included in the `_max(updatedAt)` aggregation; (5) the CredentialActionsDropdown UI (lines 69, 86-94) renders this as 'cache_last_updated'. The user sees cache status — including a 'Delete cached data' action — for a feature that is supposedly disabled, with a timestamp that is actually the migration time, not a real sync time. This combines the factory bypass with the backfill semantic issue in a way neither produces alone: the bypass alone would just query an empty table (no rows when feature is off), and the backfill alone would only mislead about freshness for active features. Together they create phantom cache status for a disabled feature, confusing users and potentially triggering unnecessary deleteCache calls (which, per the critical compound finding, are themselves no-ops). Unlike the backfill issue in isolation (which self-corrects after the first genuine post-migration write), this compound NEVER self-corrects: the flag-off state prevents the very writes that would refresh the timestamp, leaving the migration timestamp permanently frozen in the UI.
findings.evidence: CalendarCache.init (packages/features/calendar-cache/calendar-cache.ts:22-29): `if (isCalendarCacheEnabledGlobally) return new CalendarCacheRepository(calendar); return new CalendarCacheRepositoryMock();`. connectedCalendars.handler.ts:28 bypasses with `const cacheRepository = new CalendarCacheRepository();`. migration.sql:9: `ALTER TABLE "CalendarCache" ADD COLUMN "updatedAt" TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW();` — backfills all existing rows. calendar-cache.repository.ts:173-188: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds uses `_max: { updatedAt: true }` with no `expiresAt` filter. CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx:69: `hasCache = isGoogleCalendar && cacheUpdatedAt` — any non-null cacheUpdatedAt triggers the cache status UI.
findings.suggestion: Replace `new CalendarCacheRepository()` in connectedCalendars.handler.ts:28 with `await CalendarCache.init(null)` to respect the feature flag. Additionally, add an `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` filter to the groupBy query in getCacheStatusByCredentialIds (calendar-cache.repository.ts:173-188) so expired/orphaned rows are excluded from the freshness calculation, consistent with getCachedAvailability (line 121-129) which already applies this filter.
findings.title: Feature-flag bypass plus backfill migration surfaces phantom cache status for disabled feature

findings.blocking_reason: The finding is about pattern consistency with a feature-flag factory; the reviewer themselves concede the deleteCache bypass is not harmful in practice, and the connectedCalendars stale-UI concern is a behavioral inconsistency, not a build break, security issue, data loss, API contract break, or demonstrated regression.
findings.body: deleteCacheHandler uses `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany({ where: { credentialId } })` directly, bypassing the CalendarCache.init / CalendarCache.initFromCredentialId factory (calendar-cache.ts:22-29). The factory checks `isCalendarCacheEnabledGlobally` via FeaturesRepository.checkIfFeatureIsEnabledGlobally('calendar-cache') and returns a CalendarCacheRepositoryMock (no-op) when the feature is globally disabled. The canonical call sites — CalendarService.ts:463,616,981 (CalendarCache.init(null)), calendar-cache/api/cron.ts:80,124 (initFromCredentialId) — all go through this factory. When the 'calendar-cache' feature flag is globally disabled, the canonical pattern would return CalendarCacheRepositoryMock, whose deleteManyByCredential() is a no-op — meaning cache deletion would be a no-op (correct, because the Mock doesn't write cache rows either). But deleteCacheHandler bypasses the factory and hits prisma directly, so it would actually DELETE rows even when the feature is disabled. While this is not harmful in practice (toggleFeatureFlag.handler.ts:34 already deletes ALL rows when the feature is disabled, so there are no rows to delete), it creates a pattern inconsistency: the handler's behavior diverges from the canonical factory-gated pattern. More concerningly, the companion handler connectedCalendars.handler.ts:28 also bypasses the factory with `new CalendarCacheRepository()` — this IS harmful because getCacheStatusByCredentialIds would query the DB and return real cache status data even when the feature is globally disabled, potentially showing stale UI state that contradicts the feature flag. The ICalendarCacheRepository interface is also incomplete — it lacks a delete method (CalendarCacheRepositoryMock has deleteManyByCredential but the interface does not declare it), which may be why deleteCacheHandler bypassed the factory: there was no interface method to call. This suggests the interface should be extended with a delete method, and both handlers should use the factory.
findings.dimension_name: CalendarCache.init Factory Bypass — Feature Flag Ignored
findings.evidence: Factory check: calendar-cache.ts:22-29 — `const isCalendarCacheEnabledGlobally = await featureRepo.checkIfFeatureIsEnabledGlobally('calendar-cache'); if (isCalendarCacheEnabledGlobally) return new CalendarCacheRepository(calendar); return new CalendarCacheRepositoryMock();`. Canonical callers using factory: CalendarService.ts:463,616,981; calendar-cache/api/cron.ts:80,124. Bypassers: deleteCache.handler.ts:28 (prisma direct), connectedCalendars.handler.ts:28 (`new CalendarCacheRepository()` direct). Interface gap: ICalendarCacheRepository has watchCalendar, unwatchCalendar, upsertCachedAvailability, getCachedAvailability, getCacheStatusByCredentialIds — NO delete method. Mock has deleteManyByCredential at line 23 but interface doesn't declare it.
findings.suggestion: Two options: (A) Extend ICalendarCacheRepository with `deleteManyByCredential(credentialId: number): Promise<void>` (the Mock already has this method — just promote it to the interface). Then deleteCacheHandler should use `const cacheRepo = await CalendarCache.initFromCredentialId(credentialId); await cacheRepo.deleteManyByCredential(credentialId);`. This respects the feature flag and uses the canonical pattern. (B) If the intent is that cache deletion should ALWAYS work regardless of feature flag (because you want to clean up stale rows from when the feature was previously enabled), then document this explicitly and keep the direct prisma call — but connectedCalendars.handler.ts:28 should still use the factory to avoid returning stale cache status when the feature is disabled. Either way, the ICalendarCacheRepository interface should be extended with the delete method to make the contract complete.
findings.title: Handler bypasses CalendarCache.init factory — does not respect isCalendarCacheEnabledGlobally feature flag

findings.blocking_reason: Relies on implicit Prisma @updatedAt behavior and lacks explicit data — a code fragility concern, not a demonstrated breaking change, security issue, data loss, API break, or behavior regression.
findings.body:
The new `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId` method is invoked at `CalendarService.ts:1024` as `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` with an **empty `data` object**. The intent is to touch the `@updatedAt` timestamp on all selected calendars under a credential after cache refresh. However, this relies entirely on Prisma's implicit `@updatedAt` directive behavior: Prisma auto-injects `updatedAt = new Date()` into the UPDATE payload even when `data` is `{}`.

**Why this is fragile:**
1. **Silent no-op risk**: If the `@updatedAt` directive is ever removed from the `SelectedCalendar` model in `schema.prisma`, or if Prisma changes its empty-data semantics, this becomes a silent no-op — no error, no update, no timestamp change. The cache-refresh flow would appear to work but `updatedAt` would never advance, breaking any downstream logic that compares `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` to `CalendarCache.updatedAt`.
2. **Non-obvious intent**: A reader sees `updateMany(..., {})` and has no way to know the purpose is to bump `updatedAt`. The comment on line 1023 (`// Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under this credential`) helps, but the code itself doesn't express the intent.
3. **Broad blast radius**: `updateMany` with `where: { credentialId }` updates **every** selected calendar row for that credential — including event-type-level calendars that may not have been part of the availability fetch. This is a wider write than the loop on lines 1009-1021 which only processes per-eventType groups.
4. **No count verification**: The return value (count of updated rows) is discarded. If zero rows matched the `credentialId`, the caller has no signal — the cache refresh silently succeeded but no `updatedAt` was bumped.
findings.dimension_name: Coverage Gap 5 - selectedCalendar.ts and user.ts repository changes
findings.evidence:
Step 1: CalendarService.ts:1024 calls `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` with empty data object.
Step 2: selectedCalendar.ts:400-405 `updateManyByCredentialId` forwards `data` to `prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany({ where: { credentialId }, data })`.
Step 3: Prisma receives `data: {}` — the only field that gets written is the auto-injected `@updatedAt`.
Step 4: If Prisma's `@updatedAt` auto-injection is removed or the schema directive is dropped, the UPDATE becomes a no-op with no error, and `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` never advances despite cache refresh having occurred.
findings.title: updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data {} relies on implicit Prisma @updatedAt behavior

findings.blocking_reason: This is an architectural critique about bypassing abstraction layers; the finding itself admits each bypass is functionally correct and frames the concern as future maintainability, not a concrete current production impact.
findings.body: Both new handlers introduced by this PR bypass every established abstraction layer for credential access and cache management. deleteCacheHandler: (1) auth via direct `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })` bypasses CredentialRepository (F0); (2) cache delete via direct `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany` bypasses both the `CalendarCache.init` factory and `CalendarCacheRepository` (related to F2); (3) no `stopWatchingCalendarsInGoogle` / `googleChannel*` teardown bypasses the `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar` lifecycle pattern (F2). connectedCalendarsHandler: (4) `new CalendarCacheRepository()` direct construction bypasses `CalendarCache.init` factory and its `FeaturesRepository.checkIfFeatureIsEnabledGlobally("calendar-cache")` gate (F3). Each bypass is suggestion-severity in isolation — the constructor accepts `calendar: Calendar | null = null`, getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores `this.calendar`, and direct prisma auth is functionally correct. But together they constitute a structural disconnect: the PR's new cache UI surface is wired to NONE of the infrastructure every other consumer of CalendarCache/CredentialRepository uses. Any future fix to the cache lifecycle (a new required side-effect on delete, a new feature-flag-gated behavior, a new auth constraint) will NOT propagate to these handlers because they never traverse the seams where such fixes would land. The handlers will silently diverge from canonical behavior as the codebase evolves, and the divergence will be invisible to any refactor that only updates the factory/repository/service layer.
findings.evidence: deleteCache.handler.ts:17-22 — direct `prisma.credential.findFirst` (CredentialRepository bypass, F0). deleteCache.handler.ts:28-30 — direct `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany` (CalendarCache.init factory + CalendarCacheRepository bypass; no `stopWatchingCalendarsInGoogle` call, no `googleChannel*` clearing, F2). connectedCalendars.handler.ts:28-29 — `new CalendarCacheRepository()` (CalendarCache.init factory bypass, F3). Canonical factory: `CalendarCache.init(calendar)` → `FeaturesRepository.checkIfFeatureIsEnabledGlobally("calendar-cache")` → returns `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` when flag off. Canonical cache delete: `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar:947-967` pairs `calendarCache.deleteMany` with HTTP stop + googleChannel* clearing. All 4 other production call sites for `calendarCache.deleteMany` go through `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar`.
findings.suggestion: Route both handlers through the established seams: (1) `deleteCacheHandler` should call `CalendarService.unwatchCalendar` (or factor out its teardown) instead of raw `prisma.calendarCache.deleteMany`, and use `CredentialRepository` (or its authorized-find helper) instead of `prisma.credential.findFirst`; (2) `connectedCalendarsHandler` should call `CalendarCache.init(ctx.user.credentials ?? null)` instead of `new CalendarCacheRepository()`, so the feature flag is honored. This makes future cache-lifecycle fixes automatically apply to the new UI surface. If bypass is intentional for performance, document the divergence at the call site so future refactors don't assume the handlers inherit canonical behavior.
findings.title: PR's new calendar-cache handlers systematically bypass all established cache/auth abstraction layers — structurally incapable of inheriting future lifecycle fixes

findings.blocking_reason: Interface/mock drift is a code quality issue with no demonstrated breakage of build, tests, or production behavior.
findings.body: `ICalendarCacheRepository` interface drift: mock implements `deleteManyByCredential`, interface doesn't declare it, real repo doesn't implement it — three-way split that makes the mock's method dead code
findings.title: ICalendarCacheRepository interface drift

findings.blocking_reason: Missing expiresAt filter in a cache status read query may show stale timestamps but does not cause data loss, security issues, or regressions to previously working behavior.
findings.body: The `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` method queries `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy` with only `credentialId` in the where clause. It does not filter by `expiresAt` or any validity condition. If cache rows exist but have expired (past their `expiresAt` date), the method still returns their `updatedAt` timestamp, presenting stale cache data as current.
findings.evidence: repository.ts: `where: { credentialId: { in: credentialIds } }` - no `expiresAt` filter. The CalendarCache model has an `expiresAt` field that indicates cache validity.
findings.suggestion: Add `expiresAt: { gt: new Date() }` to the where clause to only show cache status for non-expired entries. Or return both the timestamp and whether the cache is expired so the UI can display accordingly.
findings.title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds doesn't filter by expiresAt - shows stale/expired cache timestamps

findings.blocking_reason: Performance suggestion with no correctness impact; an empty array query returns correct results, just with an unnecessary DB roundtrip.
findings.body: The method does not check if `credentialIds` is empty before executing the Prisma query. If called with an empty array, Prisma's `in: []` produces a query that returns no results but still hits the database. While Prisma may optimize this, it's a best practice to short-circuit.
findings.evidence: repository.ts: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(credentialIds: number[])` - no `if (credentialIds.length === 0) return [];` guard at the top.
findings.suggestion: Add early return: `if (credentialIds.length === 0) return [];` at the start of the method.
findings.title: No empty array guard in getCacheStatusByCredentialIds - unnecessary DB query

findings.blocking_reason: Code clarity concern about an empty update object; no demonstrated build break, data loss, security issue, or behavioral regression.
findings.body: After `fetchAvailability`, the code calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` with an empty data object. This relies on Prisma's `@updatedAt` auto-updating the `updatedAt` field even when no other fields are modified. The semantic intent is 'mark these calendars as just synced', but an empty update is an unclear way to express this. Additionally, Prisma's behavior with empty data in `updateMany` may vary across versions.
findings.suggestion: Either explicitly pass `{ updatedAt: new Date() }` to make the intent clear, or create a dedicated method like `touchManyByCredentialId(credentialId)` that encapsulates the 'update timestamp only' intent.
findings.title: updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data object - relies on Prisma @updatedAt auto-bump

findings.blocking_reason: Data display nuance in UI that self-corrects after first post-migration write; does not break build, tests, API contracts, or cause data loss.
findings.body: The return shape is structurally correct (TypeScript compiles, interface `Date | null` matches Prisma's conservative `_max` typing, `|| null` correctly coerces `undefined`→`null` for missing keys). However, the migration backfills `updatedAt = NOW()` for all pre-existing rows, making `_max(updatedAt)` return the migration timestamp rather than a genuine sync time for credentials with only pre-migration cache rows. The UI displays this under the `cache_last_updated` label, implying a fresh sync when the data could be stale. Self-corrects after the first post-migration cache write.
findings.title: Migration backfill of updatedAt=NOW() makes _max(updatedAt) show migration timestamp instead of genuine sync time

findings.blocking_reason: This is a UX/i18n consistency suggestion, not a build break, security issue, data loss, API break, or regression.
findings.body:
`CredentialActionsDropdown` formats the `cacheUpdatedAt` timestamp with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`, hardcoding the locale to US English. Cal.com is fully i18n'd — this same PR touched `apps/web/public/static/locales/en/common.json` to add the `cache_last_updated` translation key, and the component already calls `useLocale()` (line 37) which returns `{ t, i18n, isLocaleReady }` where `i18n.language` is the active user locale.

This is inconsistent with the established codebase pattern. At least 7 other components use `i18n.language` from `useLocale()` to drive `Intl.DateTimeFormat`:

- `packages/features/bookings/Booker/components/Header.tsx:94` — `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language ?? "en", { month: "short" })`
- `packages/features/troubleshooter/components/TroubleshooterHeader.tsx:33` — `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language, { month: "short" })`
- `packages/features/schedules/components/DateOverrideList.tsx:52,65,122` — `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language, ...)`
- `packages/features/calendars/DatePicker.tsx:326` — `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language, { month: "long" })`
- `packages/features/calendars/weeklyview/components/DateValues/index.tsx:15` — `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language, { weekday: "short" })`
- `packages/features/ee/video/ViewRecordingsDialog.tsx:46` — `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, ...)` (locale derived from i18n)

The practical impact: a user with their profile set to `fr`, `de`, `es`, `pt-BR`, etc., will see the cache timestamp rendered in US format (MM/DD/YYYY, 12-hour AM/PM) while every other timestamp in the app renders in their locale. For `pt-BR` users this is especially jarring — they expect DD/MM/YYYY 24-hour and instead see the US format right next to the `"Cache Status"` label which *is* correctly localized. It's a UX inconsistency, not a runtime failure.
findings.evidence:
Step 1: `CredentialActionsDropdown` calls `const { t } = useLocale();` at line 37, but only destructures `t` — it ignores `i18n` which carries the active locale.
Step 2: At line 89, the component calls `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" }).format(new Date(cacheUpdatedAt))` — the locale argument is the literal string `"en-US"`.
Step 3: Compare with `packages/features/bookings/Booker/components/Header.tsx:94`: `new Intl.DateTimeFormat(i18n.language ?? "en", { month: "short" })` — the canonical pattern uses `i18n.language`.
Step 4: `packages/features/troubleshooter/components/TroubleshooterHeader.tsx:33` and `packages/features/schedules/components/DateOverrideList.tsx:52,65,122` all use `i18n.language` directly with `Intl.DateTimeFormat`.
Step 5: Result — a user whose `i18n.language` is `fr`/`de`/`es`/`pt-BR` sees a US-formatted cache timestamp while the rest of the app honors their locale, producing inconsistent UX.
findings.title: Hardcoded "en-US" locale in Intl.DateTimeFormat ignores user's i18n locale

findings.blocking_reason: This is a dependency hygiene and reproducibility concern for a dev-only script; it does not break production builds, tests, or any user-facing code path.
findings.body:
The `dev:cron` script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is **not declared as a dependency anywhere** in the monorepo (verified: no `"tsx":` key in `apps/web/package.json`, root `package.json`, any `packages/*/package.json`, and 0 matches for `tsx@` in `yarn.lock`). 

Using `npx tsx` means the package is fetched on-demand from the npm registry on first run. This has three concrete consequences:

1. **Offline / air-gapped CI failure**: In environments without registry access (common in hardened CI runners, corporate proxies, or `--offline` yarn installs), `npx tsx` fails with `npm ERR! code E404` / network errors. `ts-node` was previously installed via `devDependencies` so this was not an issue.
2. **Non-reproducible builds**: `npx` resolves the latest matching version at invocation time, so the `tsx` version used by `dev:cron` is not pinned in `yarn.lock`. Two developers running the same script a week apart may get different `tsx` versions, leading to "works on my machine" transpilation differences.
3. **Hidden dependency**: The dependency graph no longer reflects that `apps/web` requires `tsx` to run its `dev:cron` script. Tooling that checks `devDependencies` to determine install requirements (e.g., Docker images pruning devDeps for production) will not know `tsx` is needed.

Note: `npx` does cache packages after first download, so the network dependency is only on first run per machine — but this does not address reproducibility or the offline-CI concern.

This change appears intentional (likely to get `tsx`'s superior ESM/TypeScript transpilation for `cron-tester.ts` which uses `import { CronJob } from "cron"`), but the dependency should be declared rather than fetched ad-hoc.
findings.evidence: Step 1: Developer runs `yarn dev:cron` in `apps/web/`. Step 2: yarn invokes the script `npx tsx cron-tester.ts` (line 11). Step 3: `npx` looks for `tsx` in local `node_modules/.bin` — not found (not in `devDependencies`, verified by grep of `apps/web/package.json` lines 154-198). Step 4: `npx` fetches `tsx` from npm registry. Step 5: In an offline environment (e.g., CI with `yarn install --offline`), this fails with a network error. Step 6: Even when online, the resolved `tsx` version is not recorded in `yarn.lock` (0 matches for `tsx@` in lockfile), so the version is non-deterministic across runs.
findings.suggestion: Add `"tsx": "^4.19.0"` (or current latest) to the `devDependencies` block of `apps/web/package.json`, then change the script to `"dev:cron": "tsx cron-tester.ts"` (drop `npx`). This makes the dependency explicit, pins the version in `yarn.lock`, and works in offline CI. Alternatively, if the team prefers keeping `npx` for zero-install convenience, document the network requirement.
findings.title: `tsx` not declared as devDependency — `npx tsx` relies on on-demand download

findings.blocking_reason: Developer convenience script path issue with no production impact; no build, test, security, or data-loss consequence.
findings.body: Line 5 sets `ENV_FILE="../.env"`. This only resolves correctly if the script is invoked from inside the `scripts/` directory (e.g., `cd scripts && ./test-gcal-webhooks.sh`). If a developer runs `bash scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh` from the repo root (the more common invocation pattern), `../.env` resolves to the parent of the repo root, not to the repo's `.env` file. The script will either silently update the wrong file (if it exists) or fail with a confusing "No such file" error from sed.
findings.suggestion: Make the path relative to the script location: `ENV_FILE="$(dirname "$0")/../.env"` or `SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"; ENV_FILE="$SCRIPT_DIR/../.env".
findings.title: ENV_FILE relative path assumes cwd is scripts/

findings.blocking_reason: Missing row-count check on delete is a code-quality/defensive-programming concern with no demonstrated production impact.
findings.body: Returns `{success: true}` even when `deleteMany` deletes 0 rows (no row-count check) — masks no-op deletes.
findings.title: Returns success even when 0 rows are deleted
